controls.statement: Generate an SBOM for every released artifact.
Include direct, transitive, runtime, operating-system, container, client, server, plugin, model, and embedded components as applicable.
Record exact versions, package identifiers, sources, hashes, relationships, licenses, and required notices.
Link the SBOM to the released artifact digest and verify it against the final package.
Ensure no undeclared or unexpected components are present.
Remove unused, unsupported, and end-of-life dependencies.
Confirm dependencies come from intended publishers and registries.
Monitor upstream advisories and continuously scan released components.
Prioritize vulnerabilities using exploitation, reachability, exposure, criticality, data sensitivity, and compensating controls.
Define remediation targets by actual risk and verify fixes or mitigations after deployment.
Maintain an emergency replacement process for compromised dependencies.
Document ownership of vendored, forked, and internally patched components.
Verify license compatibility and fulfill attribution, notice, source-offer, and redistribution obligations.
Prevent unintended inclusion of proprietary or confidential code in distributable artifacts.
Retain SBOMs for historical releases and investigations.
Certificates cover correct names and trust chains.

controls.statement: Cryptographic requirements derive from a documented threat model and data classification.
Only approved, maintained algorithms, libraries, and protocol implementations are used.
Custom cryptographic algorithms and ad hoc protocols are absent.
Encryption provides confidentiality, integrity, and authenticity as required by the threat model.
Keys are stored separately from protected data where practical.
Keys do not appear in source, logs, artifacts, frontend code, tickets, or ordinary configuration.
Rotation does not make required existing data unrecoverable.
Required keys and recovery credentials are securely included in continuity and recovery planning.
Key deletion and cryptographic-erasure behavior are defined.
Certificates, signing keys, token keys, encryption keys, and webhook keys have lifecycle owners.
Signature verification rejects inappropriate algorithms, keys, malformed input, and algorithm confusion.
Random identifiers and security tokens use cryptographically secure generation where unpredictability is required.
Sensitive plaintext is not copied unnecessarily into analytics, logs, caches, indexes, backups, or support tools.
The release is assessed against the applicable OWASP Application Security Verification Standard requirements.
Dependency, SBOM, and license analysis has run.
Secret scanning has run against current changes and relevant history.
Infrastructure, configuration, and policy analysis has run.
Deployed application and API security testing has run.
Authentication, account recovery, session, authorization, and tenant-isolation testing has run.
Injection, unsafe-input, browser, file-processing, business-logic, abuse, and fraud testing has run where applicable.
Penetration testing covers authenticated users, multiple roles, multiple tenants, APIs, administrative tools, and business logic as applicable.
Findings have owners, risk ratings, remediation targets, and retest evidence.
Relevant known-exploited vulnerabilities are blockers unless non-exposure and mitigation are convincingly demonstrated.
Unsupported and unpatchable components have explicit treatment plans.
A vulnerability-disclosure policy and security-reporting channel exist.
Security reports receive acknowledgment, triage, remediation tracking, coordinated disclosure handling, and appropriate credit.
Security monitoring covers account takeover, privilege changes, secret use, suspicious exports, abuse, fraud, and control tampering.
Incident severity levels and declaration authority are defined.

controls.statement: Define security objectives from business context, assets, threats, legal duties, contracts, and risk appetite.
Assign accountable owners for information, services, identities, systems, controls, vulnerabilities, and incidents.
Maintain a current inventory of assets, data, interfaces, dependencies, identities, secrets, and externally exposed surfaces.
Use a consistent risk method that records threat, vulnerability, likelihood, impact, existing controls, residual risk, and owner.
Prioritize based on realistic exploitability, exposure, reachability, user harm, business impact, and control strength.
Select controls proportionate to risk and verify they operate in the actual environment.
Separate policy requirements from implementation guidance and document justified tailoring.
Define minimum baselines for products, environments, suppliers, identities, endpoints, and data classes.
Require independent review for material security decisions and exceptions.
Make security exceptions time-bounded with compensating controls, monitoring, and automatic expiry.
Integrate security objectives into funding, planning, requirements, architecture, procurement, delivery, and operations.
Protect security staff independence while keeping product teams accountable for owned risk.
Measure control effectiveness, detection, remediation, recurrence, and risk reduction rather than finding counts alone.
Review inherited provider controls and identify customer responsibilities explicitly.
Maintain vulnerability disclosure, researcher communication, and coordinated remediation processes.
Use incidents, threat intelligence, exercises, audits, and near misses to update controls.
Prevent security work from being deferred indefinitely as nonfunctional or post-launch.
Review risk after material scope, data, identity, supplier, exposure, architecture, or threat changes.
Maintain executive visibility of risk that exceeds approved tolerance.
Do not claim security based solely on compliance, certification, penetration tests, or absence of known findings.
Define role-specific secure-development responsibilities and competency requirements.
Protect source, build, test, artifact, deployment, signing, and production environments according to their trust.
Translate threat models and security objectives into traceable requirements and verification.
Use approved patterns for identity, authorization, input handling, secrets, cryptography, logging, and error responses.
Review security-sensitive architecture and code with qualified independent reviewers.
Scan source, dependencies, secrets, infrastructure, configuration, and artifacts using maintained rules.
Treat automated findings as evidence inputs requiring triage, not automatic truth or automatic dismissal.
Perform manual testing for business logic, authorization, identity recovery, tenant isolation, and abuse cases.
Verify the exact release artifact and configuration rather than only source branches.
Generate and retain provenance, dependency inventory, SBOM, signatures, test evidence, and approvals.
Define release gates based on risk, exploit activity, exposure, and remediation capability.
Keep a secure emergency patch and release path that preserves traceability and review.
Monitor released components for newly disclosed vulnerabilities and compromised suppliers.
Maintain response procedures for leaked secrets, malicious packages, build compromise, and signing-key compromise.
Convert findings and incidents into requirements, tests, patterns, training, and architecture improvements.
Review security debt and unsupported components as planned lifecycle obligations.
Apply equivalent controls to scripts, migrations, infrastructure, pipelines, internal tools, and low-code assets.
Ensure suppliers can provide sufficient security evidence and notification.
Track security requirements through deprecation and retirement, including data and credential cleanup.
Measure security outcomes without rewarding concealment or excessive low-value findings.
Define the system, release, feature, or workflow in scope and its assumptions.
Inventory assets, sensitive operations, users, administrators, service identities, suppliers, and attackers.
Map entry points, data flows, trust boundaries, stores, queues, callbacks, support paths, and recovery mechanisms.
Include accidental misuse, malicious outsiders, compromised users, insiders, compromised suppliers, automation, and physical access where relevant.
Model identity spoofing, tampering, disclosure, denial, privilege escalation, repudiation, fraud, and business-logic abuse.
Model cross-user, cross-tenant, cross-environment, and cross-region isolation failure.
Model account recovery, support intervention, impersonation, and administrative override.
Model dependency, package, build, pipeline, artifact, secret, and control-plane compromise.
Model privacy harm, surveillance, reidentification, inference, coercion, and harmful secondary use.
Model resource exhaustion, economic denial, quota abuse, scraping, spam, and automation.
Model data corruption, replay, duplication, ordering, race, rollback, and recovery attacks.
Model observability, alerting, backup, and incident-response blind spots.
Rank scenarios using evidence and local context rather than generic labels alone.
Convert every material scenario into prevention, detection, response, test, and residual-risk decisions.
Validate assumptions with architecture, source, configuration, deployment, and operator evidence.
Use adversarial walkthroughs and abuse stories with product, security, engineering, operations, privacy, and support participants.
Update the model after material design, integration, identity, data, deployment, or incident changes.
Track unresolved threats with owners and deadlines.
Test mitigations against bypass and alternate paths.
Preserve the threat model as a living decision artifact, not a one-time diagram.
Use an explicit application-security verification level appropriate to impact and exposure.
Enforce authentication and authorization at every trusted operation and resource boundary.
Deny by default and prevent object, function, property, and tenant authorization bypass.
Validate and normalize untrusted input at trusted boundaries.
Use parameterized or safe structured APIs for interpreters, queries, commands, templates, paths, and parsers.
Encode output for the exact destination context and sanitize intentionally allowed active content.
Protect state-changing browser operations against cross-site request forgery.
Prevent server-side request forgery through destination, scheme, redirect, DNS, and metadata controls.
Prevent insecure deserialization, unsafe dynamic evaluation, parser ambiguity, path traversal, and archive traversal.
Use safe error handling that does not reveal internals or convert security failure into success.
Protect session identifiers, tokens, recovery material, and sensitive state throughout their lifecycle.
Apply rate, quota, anti-automation, and resource limits at meaningful identities and operations.
Protect uploads, downloads, generated files, and derived content through validation, isolation, access control, and cleanup.
Apply browser isolation and transport controls appropriate to content and trust.
Keep sensitive data out of URLs, logs, analytics, caches, client storage, and support tools unless explicitly justified.
Test business invariants, race conditions, duplicate requests, workflow skipping, and partial failure.
Protect administrative and support actions with stronger controls and audit.
Review third-party scripts, components, integrations, and redirects as part of the application attack surface.
Use production-safe monitoring for authentication anomalies, access denials, control bypass, abuse, and data exfiltration.
Retest security after material fixes, configuration changes, migrations, and platform updates.
Inventory human, service, workload, device, emergency, supplier, and anonymous identities.
Assign each identity a unique accountable owner and purpose.
Use assurance proportional to account-compromise impact and transaction risk.
Require phishing-resistant authentication for privileged and high-impact access where feasible.
Protect enrollment, recovery, authenticator replacement, and identity linking at least as strongly as normal authentication.
Use least privilege, separation of duties, and time-bounded elevation.
Avoid shared accounts; where unavoidable, control, attribute, rotate, and review their use.
Use short-lived, scoped workload credentials rather than embedded long-lived secrets.
Verify issuer, audience, subject, signature, algorithm, time, nonce, state, and token type.
Keep delegated authorization scopes minimal and consent meaningful.
Revoke sessions, tokens, keys, connections, and cached permissions promptly after access changes.
Review access periodically according to impact and event-triggered changes.
Automate joiner, mover, leaver, supplier, tenant, and service-account lifecycle where reliable.
Protect break-glass access, test it, alert on use, and require retrospective review.
Log authentication, recovery, privilege, access-policy, impersonation, and sensitive-action events.
Detect credential stuffing, brute force, token replay, impossible use, dormant accounts, and anomalous privilege.
Prevent identity existence disclosure and social-engineering bypass through support channels.
Use independent approval for high-impact access grants and destination changes.
Ensure authorization survives background processing, caching, search, export, and data replication.
Remove orphaned identities, keys, roles, groups, sessions, and entitlements.
Inventory passwords, API keys, tokens, certificates, signing keys, encryption keys, recovery codes, and connection secrets.
Assign every secret an owner, purpose, scope, environment, consumer, creation date, rotation policy, and revocation path.
Store secrets in an approved system designed for access control, audit, and lifecycle management.
Use workload identity and short-lived credentials instead of static secrets where supported.
Keep secrets out of source, history, artifacts, images, frontend bundles, tickets, chat, documentation, tests, analytics, and logs.
Use separate secrets across environments, applications, tenants, and purposes where compromise isolation requires it.
Grant secret access to the smallest identity and operation scope.
Authenticate secret consumers and protect delivery in transit and at rest.
Avoid passing secrets through command lines, URLs, process listings, or broadly inherited environment state where exposed.
Rotate secrets automatically where safe and test rotation before relying on it.
Support emergency revocation and replacement without an uncontrolled full outage.
Monitor retrieval, failure, unusual use, stale versions, expiry, and rotation drift.
Invalidate old versions after migration and verify no consumers remain.
Scan current content and history for accidental disclosure.
Treat deletion from source as insufficient after exposure; rotate or revoke the secret.
Protect backups and recovery material containing secrets.
Control and review break-glass secrets separately.
Avoid sharing secrets between human and machine use.
Redact secrets consistently in errors, traces, crash dumps, support bundles, and diagnostics.
Exercise compromise scenarios for production credentials and signing keys.
Inventory source repositories, build systems, runners, package sources, registries, artifact stores, signers, deployment systems, and suppliers.
Protect repository, pipeline, artifact, and signing administration with strong identity and least privilege.
Require reviewed source and protected pipeline definitions for trusted releases.
Separate untrusted contribution workflows from release secrets and trusted builders.
Pin and verify build inputs sufficiently to prevent unexpected substitution.
Use isolated, ephemeral, or clean build environments appropriate to risk.
Generate immutable artifact digests and provenance tied to exact source and build inputs.
Sign or attest release artifacts and verify before promotion and deployment.
Build once and promote the same artifact through environments.
Generate an SBOM for the final artifact, including transitive and embedded components.
Verify artifact content against declared inputs and detect unexpected files or dependencies.
Protect caches from cross-trust poisoning and stale unverified substitution.
Restrict build and deploy network access and credentials to minimum need.
Prevent pull-request or untrusted jobs from modifying trusted release state.
Monitor dependencies and build components for compromise, vulnerability, and ownership change.
Retain previous trusted artifacts, provenance, and reproducible rebuild capability.
Define revocation, rebuild, resigning, redistributing, and customer-notification procedures.
Test supply-chain incident response, including compromised package, runner, registry, and signing key.
Assess supplier security evidence and customer-responsibility boundaries.
Preserve chain-of-custody evidence from source to deployed artifact.
Define test scope from the threat model, architecture, data, roles, exposure, and business consequences.
Map applicable security requirements to test procedures and evidence.
Use complementary source, composition, secret, infrastructure, configuration, artifact, and deployed-behavior analysis.
Test unauthenticated, authenticated, privileged, support, service, and cross-tenant perspectives as applicable.
Test normal, alternate, error, recovery, rate, race, replay, and workflow-bypass paths.
Test identity enrollment, login, federation, recovery, authenticator change, session, and logout.
Test object, property, function, bulk, search, export, background, and administrative authorization.
Test injection, unsafe parsing, request forgery, file handling, browser boundaries, and transport configuration.
Test business abuse, fraud, automation, resource exhaustion, and economic attacks.
Verify findings manually when automated confidence is insufficient.
Record exact environment, artifact, configuration, accounts, data, methods, limitations, and evidence.
Protect testing from damaging production data, availability, privacy, or third parties.
Require independent penetration testing for high-impact or externally required systems.
Retest remediations and alternate bypass paths.
Convert confirmed findings into durable regression tests where practical.
Prioritize findings using local exploitability, reachability, exposure, impact, and controls.
Track false-positive rationales and accepted risk with evidence and expiry.
Review testing blind spots and inaccessible components explicitly.
Measure escape and recurrence rather than only scan volume.
Verify security controls continuously after deployment where safe.
Define high-value assets, attack paths, control failures, and abuse behaviors that require detection.
Collect sufficient authentication, authorization, privilege, configuration, secret, data-access, export, and administrative events.
Preserve actor, target, tenant, source, time, outcome, reason, correlation, and release context.
Protect telemetry integrity, availability, access, retention, and time synchronization.
Minimize sensitive content while retaining evidence needed for investigation.
Develop detections from threat scenarios and observed attacker behavior rather than generic log availability.
Define expected false-positive, false-negative, latency, and coverage characteristics.
Test detections through simulation, purple-team exercises, and known benign edge cases.
Route alerts to accountable responders with severity, context, and actionable runbooks.
